claims.title: Climate change/drought was a primary contributing factor
claims.desc: Paleoclimate proxies show severe multi-decadal drought across the Eastern Mediterranean ~1200–1150 BCE, likely stressing agricultural output and population stability.
claims.fc: If high-resolution climate records from the period show no significant drought signal, or if drought postdates the destruction layers by more than a generation, the climate role weakens substantially.

audit.notes: Demo data. Requires expert review before use.

claims.title: Sea Peoples invasion was a direct cause of widespread destruction
claims.desc: Egyptian texts and archaeology document Sea Peoples attacks, but whether they caused the collapse or exploited an already-collapsing system remains contested.
claims.fc: If destruction layers consistently predate Sea Peoples activity at the same sites, their causal role is weakened. If aDNA shows Sea Peoples were already present before destructions, the 'invasion' framing weakens.
claims.oc: Popular narrative often treats Sea Peoples as the primary cause; evidence supports them as one actor among several.

claims.title: Palace economy fragility made cascading collapse inevitable
claims.desc: LBA palatial economies were highly interconnected and specialized, with little redundancy. A threshold disruption in one node could propagate systemically.
claims.fc: If societies with equally interconnected economies survived the same period intact, the fragility-specific explanation weakens. Comparative cases (e.g., Egypt) must be explained.

claims.title: Internal rebellions and social upheaval contributed to collapse
claims.desc: Some texts hint at lower-class or pastoral uprisings. Collapse of redistributive palace economies may have triggered internal resistance.
claims.fc: If no textual or archaeological evidence of internal conflict is found at collapse sites, and if external disruption accounts for all destruction patterns, internal rebellion is weakened as a factor.

claims.title: Earthquakes contributed to specific destruction events
claims.desc: Seismic evidence has been proposed for several destructions (e.g., Tiryns, Mycenae). However, earthquake-caused destruction is only confirmed at a subset of sites.
claims.fc: If seismological and archaeoseismic analysis shows no earthquake events coincident with the main destruction horizon, the earthquake factor is limited to isolated cases, not a systemic cause.

claims.title: Trade network disruption preceded and amplified political collapse
claims.desc: LBA texts show evidence of disrupted tin and copper supply before destruction layers. Without metal, palace economies could not maintain military and administrative capacity.
claims.fc: If luxury metal supply continued normally until the destruction events, or if destruction predates trade disruption, this sequence-based hypothesis weakens.

claims.title: Multiple simultaneous stressors made recovery impossible
claims.desc: Current scholarly consensus holds that no single cause explains the collapse. Climate stress, migration, trade disruption, and internal pressure interacted to push interconnected systems past recovery thresholds.
claims.fc: If a single-factor explanation (climate alone, or Sea Peoples alone) is shown to account for the full spatial and temporal pattern of collapses with no residual, the multi-causal model loses its key advantage.

claims.title: Mycenaeans/Aegeans constituted part of the Sea Peoples
claims.desc: Some aDNA and cultural evidence links Sea Peoples-associated populations to Aegean origins. However, the Sea Peoples were likely heterogeneous, not a single ethnic group.
claims.fc: If aDNA from Sea Peoples-associated Levantine Iron Age I populations shows no Aegean ancestry signal, the Mycenaean-component hypothesis weakens significantly.
claims.oc: Identifying any group as 'the Sea Peoples' is an overclaim — the term covers multiple distinct groups.
